title: Hex encoding hand-rolled four times in three different idioms
description:
The same byte-slice-to-lowercase-hex conversion appears four times, written three different ways:

- hire-core/src/pseudonym.rs:18-22 — `okm.iter().fold(String::with_capacity(64), |mut s, b| { use std::fmt::Write as _; write!(s, "{b:02x}").unwrap(); s })`
- hire-core/src/consumer.rs:50-54 — byte-for-byte the same fold, inlined inside a match arm
- hire-attestors/src/did_key.rs:39 — `hash[..8].iter().map(|b| format!("{b:02x}")).collect()`
- hire-attestors/src/fido2.rs:52 — same `map(format!).collect()`

Three problems:
1. The `fold` variants use `write!` into a `String` and `.unwrap()` the `fmt::Result` — a `Result` unwrap in non-test code for an operation that cannot fail, and the noise of a mid-expression `use` statement.
2. The `map(|b| format!(...)).collect()` variants allocate a separate `String` per byte — 8 allocations to produce 16 characters.
3. Four copies means four places to check when the encoding matters, and it does matter: these strings go into SPIFFE ID paths (`did/{short}`, `fido2/{path_hash}`) and HKDF selector keys, where a casing or width change is a silent identity change.

Fix: one `fn hex(bytes: &[u8]) -> String` in hire-core, used by all four. Simplest correct body is the `with_capacity` + `for` loop pushing two chars, no `fmt` machinery and no per-byte allocation. Adding the `hex` crate would also do it, but a six-line function avoids the dependency.
